Empirical Research Plan  
“Do Merger Waves Spread through Supply-Chain Links?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Core idea  
Treat the onset of a merger wave in an “origin” industry as an exogenous
shock and ask whether industries that buy from (or sell to) that origin
industry experience a subsequent increase in their own M&A activity that
is proportional to the economic strength of the link.

Method  
A difference-in-differences (DiD) design with a continuous treatment
intensity, combined with a shift–share (Bartik-type) instrument to deal
with any remaining endogeneity of link strength.

• Panel unit = industry-year (4-digit SIC × calendar year).  
• Main specification (reduced form):

     M&A_intensity_it = β Exposure_it + γ_i + δ_t + X_it′θ + ε_it

where Exposure_it ≡ Σ_j (Link_ij × Wave_jt–1).  
• 2SLS robustness: First stage uses the same shift–share variable
constructed from only those origin-industries whose waves are plausibly
exogenous to industry i (e.g., regulation shocks specific to j).

Why appropriate?  
(i) The timing of wave onsets is lumpy, often driven by regulatory or
technological shocks internal to the origin industry but unrelated to
idiosyncratic conditions in its suppliers/customers.  
(ii) Input–output link weights are measured *pre-treatment* (e.g., 1986
IO matrix) and are thus predetermined.  
(iii) Industry and year fixed effects absorb time-invariant differences
and common macro trends.  
(iv) Pre-trend/event-study tests are feasible to validate parallel
trends.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (continuous)  
Exposure_it = Σ_j (Link_ij × Wave_jt–1)  
• Wave_jt = 1 if industry j is in a Harford-style merger wave in year t,
0 otherwise.  
• Link_ij = dollar share of industry i’s purchases (or sales) coming
from j, averaged over 1986–1988 IO tables.

Interpretation: percentage of industry i’s input (or output) that comes
from industries currently undergoing a wave.

Control units  
Industries with zero (or very small) Link_ij to any wave industry form
the counterfactual. In practice the DiD with exposure intensity and
industry fixed effects uses *all* industries; those with Exposure = 0
serve as implicit controls.

Treatment timing  
Year immediately after the origin industry enters a wave. To avoid
mechanical simultaneity, we lag Wave by one year.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends  
Absent a wave in linked industries, high-link and low-link industries
would have followed parallel M&A trajectories.

Plausibility: We can test for differential pre-trends in an event-study
framework; macro controls and industry FE help.

A2. Link Independence  
IO links are predetermined and not themselves chosen in anticipation of
future merger waves during 1986–2010.

Plausibility: Trade patterns at 4-digit SIC evolve slowly; using the
1986–88 IO matrix (pre-sample) strengthens the case.

A3. No Simultaneous Common Shock Bias  
The origin-industry shock that triggers its own wave does not
simultaneously affect M&A in downstream industries *except* through the
supply-chain channel.

Plausibility: Many wave onsets are caused by industry-specific events
(deregulation of airlines, telecom, banking). We will control for
broad 2-digit-year shocks.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA)  
The only spillovers to industry i come through the weighted exposure
variable, not through higher-order, unmeasured networks.

Plausibility: Second-round effects are likely small over one-year
horizons; we can include two-year lags as robustness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Common Macro or Capital-Market Shocks  
Macro booms could raise both wave probability and downstream M&A.

Fix – Year fixed effects (δ_t) plus controls: GDP growth, credit-spread
shocks. Event-study pre-trends to verify.

T2. Reverse Causality  
Downstream industries might initiate mergers first, which then lead to
upstream waves.

Fix – Lag treatment by one year; replicate with two-year lag. Drop
years in which downstream industry itself is in a wave at t–1.

T3. Measurement Error in IO Links  
IO tables are noisy, causing attenuation bias.

Fix – Use averaged 1986–1988 matrix; collapse to top-quartile links for
binary treatment as robustness; instrumental-variable approach with
binary HighLink dummy × Wave_jt as instrument.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---- 0. Libraries ----
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)     # fast high-dim FE regressions
library(lmtest)     # Wald tests
library(sandwich)   # robust vcov

# ---- 1. Load data ----
ma   <- read_csv("SDC_industry_year.csv")      # industry-year #deals, wave flag
links<- read_csv("IO_link_matrix.csv")         # 4dig_i,4dig_j,link_share
controls <- read_csv("Compustat_controls.csv") # industry-year financials

# ---- 2. Construct variables ----
# a) Exposure_it = Σ_j link_ij * Wave_jt_minus1
wave <- ma %>% select(industry_j = sic4, year, wave_j = wave)
exposure <- links %>%
   left_join(wave, by = c("industry_j" = "industry_j")) %>%
   mutate(year = year + 1) %>%                     # lag by one year
   mutate(weighted_wave = link_share * wave_j) %>%
   group_by(industry_i, year) %>%
   summarise(exposure = sum(weighted_wave, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# b) Dependent variable: M&A intensity (= log(1 + #deals))
y <- ma %>%
   mutate(ma_intensity = log1p(num_deals)) %>%
   select(industry_i = sic4, year, ma_intensity)

# ---- 3. Merge analysis data set ----
panel <- y %>%
   left_join(exposure, by = c("industry_i","year")) %>%
   left_join(controls,  by = c("industry_i","year")) %>%
   mutate(exposure = replace_na(exposure, 0))

# ---- 4. Main specification ----
main_mod <- feols(ma_intensity ~ exposure + gdp_growth + credit_spread |
                    industry_i + year, data = panel, cluster = ~industry_i)
summary(main_mod)

# ---- 5. Event-study (pre-trend check) ----
panel <- panel %>%
  group_by(industry_i) %>%
  mutate(first_high = min(year[exposure>0], na.rm = TRUE),
         rel_year = year - first_high) %>% ungroup()

es_mod <- feols(ma_intensity ~ i(rel_year, ref = -1) |
                  industry_i + year, data = panel %>% filter(rel_year>=-5 & rel_year<=5),
                cluster = ~industry_i)
iplot(es_mod)

# ---- 6. Robustness: 2SLS with shift-share IV ----
# instrument = exposure constructed from *exogenous* wave industries
exogenous <- read_csv("exogenous_waves.csv") # indicator for deregulation-driven waves
exposure_iv <- links %>%
   left_join(exogenous, by = c("industry_j"="sic4")) %>%
   filter(exog_wave_j == 1) %>%
   mutate(year = year + 1,
          w_wave = link_share * wave_j) %>%
   group_by(industry_i, year) %>%
   summarise(iv_exposure = sum(w_wave, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")

panel <- panel %>% left_join(exposure_iv, by=c("industry_i","year"))

iv_mod <- feols(ma_intensity ~ 1 | industry_i + year |
                  exposure ~ iv_exposure, data = panel, cluster = ~industry_i)
summary(iv_mod)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Direction: β > 0. A one-standard-deviation increase in Exposure (≈5 ppt
of purchases coming from a wave origin) should increase downstream
M&A_intensity by roughly 10–15 percent (elasticity ≈ 0.10–0.15). Stock
returns of customers/suppliers around deal announcements should be
positive if supply-chain synergies dominate, negative if bargaining
power dominates—an empirical question.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1=satisfied, 0=concern)
1. Credible exogenous shock:                   0.8  
2. Parallel pre-trends verified:               0.8  
3. No spillover beyond measured links:         0.6  
4. Measurement reliability of key vars:        0.7  
5. Robust standard errors/clustering:          1.0  
Overall: 3.9 / 5

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan leverages well-documented exogenous variation in merger wave
timing and the fixed, economically meaningful structure of supply-chain
links to make progress on the causal question of cross-industry M&A
spillovers.
